story: Your friend Jake DMs you on Instagram saying he accidentally reported your account. He sends a link that looks like Instagram and says to click it before your account is deleted.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Click the link – you do not want to lose your account.
option_b: Message Jake on a different app to confirm he sent it.
option_c: Ask for the link to be sent again.
option_d: Delete the DM and temporarily deactivate your account.
explanation: Hacked accounts are used to send phishing links to friends. The message may look genuine but Jake's account could be compromised. Always verify urgent requests through a separate channel such as a text or phone call before clicking any link.

story: You post a photo of your new school ID badge on your public story. It shows your full name, photo, and school logo.
question: What is the main risk?
option_a: None – it is just school info.
option_b: Strangers can learn your name, school, and possibly your location.
option_c: Your school might be angry about it.
option_d: It violates the platform's terms of service.
explanation: Posting your school ID publicly gives strangers your full name, what you look like, and where you go to school. This information combined with your profile can reveal where you will be every day. Never post ID cards, tickets, or documents publicly.

story: A TikTok video claims you can get free Spotify Premium for one year. You just need to enter your email and Spotify password on a website that looks real.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Use a password you do not care about.
option_b: Report the video – it is a phishing scam.
option_c: Try it – you can always change your password after.
option_d: Use a temporary email address to sign up safely.
explanation: Free offers that require your login credentials are phishing scams. Even if the site looks exactly like Spotify, you are handing your username and password to criminals. They can then access your account and any other accounts where you use the same password.

story: You are tagged in an embarrassing photo. Someone messages you privately threatening to share it widely unless you pay them money.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Pay once and then block them.
option_b: Screenshot everything, block the user, and tell a trusted adult.
option_c: Ignore it – they probably will not share it.
option_d: Delete your social media account to stop them.
explanation: This is digital blackmail, also called sextortion or cyber extortion. Never pay – it almost always leads to more demands. Document all messages as evidence, block the person, and immediately report it to a parent, teacher, or the platform.

story: You receive an email that looks exactly like it came from Apple. It says your iCloud is 99% full and asks for your Apple ID and password to prevent data loss.
question: What is the safest action?
option_a: Click the link and log in – it looks real.
option_b: Open your iCloud settings directly through the app, not the email.
option_c: Reply to the email asking if it is a scam.
option_d: Forward the email to Apple customer support.
explanation: Phishing emails are designed to look exactly like official emails from trusted companies. Always go directly to the official app or website by typing the address yourself, never by clicking a link in an email. This is one of the most common ways accounts get hacked.

story: A friend messages you on Discord saying they accidentally sent a two-factor authentication code to your phone number and needs you to read it to them.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Give the code – it is your friend asking.
option_b: Call your friend to confirm it is really them before doing anything.
option_d: Send only the first digit to check if they can figure out the rest.
explanation: Two-factor authentication codes should never be shared with anyone, including friends. Scammers often hack an account and then pretend to be the owner to get the 2FA code from a contact. Always verify by calling the friend directly before taking any action.

story: A new classmate you have only known for two days asks to share live locations on Snapchat so you can hang out after school.
question: What is the best choice?
option_b: Wait until you know them much better in real life.
option_c: Share it but only for one hour.
option_d: Share your location but set it to a nearby wrong location first.
explanation: Sharing your live location means someone can always see exactly where you are. This is a serious privacy risk with someone you barely know. Build trust in person over time before sharing real-time location data with anyone.

story: You read that a game you play had a data breach. Your email and hashed password may have been leaked.
question: What should you do immediately?
option_a: Nothing – the password was hashed so it is safe.
option_b: Change your password on that game and on any other site where you used the same password.
option_d: Create a new email account and transfer your game progress.
explanation: Hashed passwords can still be cracked, especially simple ones. More importantly, if you used the same password on multiple sites, attackers will try it everywhere. This is called credential stuffing. Always use a unique password for each account.

story: A message says that if you do not forward it to ten friends tonight, your account will be hacked.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Forward it – just to be safe.
option_b: Delete it – this is a hoax designed to spread fear and spam.
option_c: Send it to only five friends as a compromise.
option_d: Forward it with a warning note attached.
explanation: Chain messages that threaten you with hacking unless you forward them are fake. They are designed to spread spam and create fear. Hackers do not actually track whether you forwarded a message. Delete it and do not send it to others.

story: An unknown account offers you a social media assistant job paying £300 a week just to post links. They ask for your full name, address, and bank details via DM for payment.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Give fake details to stay safe.
option_b: Report and block – legitimate jobs do not ask for bank details via DM.
option_c: Ask for a video interview before giving any information.
option_d: Ask for payment via PayPal first before sharing bank details.
explanation: This is a job scam. It is used to steal your identity, your money, or to involve you in illegal money laundering. Legitimate employers never request your bank account or home address through a social media DM. Report and block immediately.

story: A YouTuber you trust promotes a free VPN saying it makes you completely anonymous and impossible to hack.
question: What should you think about this claim?
option_a: The YouTuber would not lie – trust the recommendation.
option_b: Free VPNs often sell your data, and no tool makes you 100% anonymous.
option_c: Install it – even basic protection is better than nothing.
option_d: A paid VPN is always 100% safe and anonymous instead.
explanation: Free VPN services frequently earn money by logging and selling your browsing data to advertisers or third parties – the opposite of what they promise. No technology makes you truly anonymous. Be critical of influencer endorsements which are often paid promotions.

story: You add a new person to your private story. The next day, screenshots appear in a large group chat and you are humiliated.
question: What is the most important lesson here?
option_a: Never use private stories at all.
option_b: Only add people you completely trust in real life, and assume anything digital can be shared.
option_c: Report the person and move on.
option_d: Switch your story settings to followers-only from now on.
explanation: Digital trust is fragile. Anyone who can view your content can screenshot and share it. A 'private' setting only limits who can see it initially. Never post anything you would not be comfortable with becoming public, and be very selective about who you grant access to.

story: You see a poster at a bus stop saying scan to win a free phone. You scan the QR code and it asks for your phone number and email address.
question: What is the danger?
option_a: None – QR codes are always safe.
option_b: It could lead to a phishing site or download malware onto your device.
option_c: It is only dangerous if you also enter payment information.
option_d: It is only dangerous if you enter payment and personal details together.
explanation: QR codes are simply links in a different form. A malicious QR code can redirect you to a phishing website designed to steal your information, or it can trigger an automatic download of malware. Be very cautious about scanning random QR codes in public places.

story: A stranger messages you claiming someone is using your photos on a fake account. They provide a link for you to click to see and report it.
question: What should you do?
option_a: Click the link – you want to protect your photos.
option_b: Search for your name on the platform yourself instead of clicking the link.
option_c: Ask the stranger to send screenshots instead.
option_d: Message the stranger back to get the link resent.
explanation: Scammers use fear about your reputation to make you click dangerous links. The link could lead to a phishing page or install malware. Always investigate a claim directly through the official platform yourself rather than through a link a stranger provides.

story: Someone creates a fake anonymous account and posts mean things about you in a large group chat. Nobody knows who it is.
question: What is the most effective first step?
option_b: Screenshot everything, leave the chat, and report to the platform and a school counsellor.
option_c: Create your own anonymous account to fight back.
option_d: Create a new account with your real name to prove the fake one is wrong.
explanation: Responding angrily or retaliating gives the bully attention and can escalate the situation. The right approach is to document evidence with screenshots, leave the group, report the account to the platform, and tell a trusted adult such as a school counsellor or parent.
